title: How to safely connect an LLM to a live broker (The Zero-Trust Pipeline)
author: DTAKthatGuy
selftext:
Letting an AI model write raw code to execute trades is a disaster waiting to happen. In live capital environments, you need strict boundaries between probabilistic reasoning and deterministic execution:

1. **Structured Tool Calling (MCP):** The agent never outputs freeform text. It fills out a pre-validated digital ticket (Ticker, Action, Quantity, Limit Price, Stop Loss).
2. **Pre-Trade Price Collars:** The system compares the proposed price against the live NBBO spread. If the agent hallucinates a price outside current market bounds, the ticket is instantly killed.
3. **Credential Isolation:** API keys never enter the prompt window. An independent execution daemon signs and dispatches the order behind the scenes.
4. **Exchange-Side Brackets:** Always submit orders with attached bracket stops so open trades remain protected even if your local server drops offline.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good list, and keeping the keys out of the prompt window is the one I'd put first. Two things I'd add: use keys that can only trade and can't withdraw, so even a leaked key can't move funds out, and put a daily loss cap and max order size in the execution layer where the model can't change them. It also helps to run the whole pipeline on paper first and check that the collar actually rejects bad tickets. Cymetica's Exchange Connections works on the same idea, with trade-only keys on your own exchange account.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body: I would add an acknowledgement/fill state machine. A request timing out is not proof the order failed; resending it without reconciliation can double the position. Test disconnects after submission, partial fills, cancel/replace races and bracket rejection, and make the execution service fail closed when account state is uncertain. QATS team here; this is the execution boundary we would want to inspect in any agent integration. Does your test harness include those failure sequences, or only invalid order tickets?
